Research case study / PRISM

Why does the
backbone matter?

Investigating how minimum spanning tree and odometric backbones shape the optimization landscape and the final connectivity of sparse SLAM pose graphs.

SLAMSpectral Graph TheoryFrank–WolfePose-Graph Sparsification
01 / The problem

Same budget. Different outcome.

A pose graph represents robot poses as vertices and relative-pose measurements as edges. Sparsification reduces computational cost by retaining a limited set of informative measurements while preserving connectivity.

MAC begins with a connected backbone, either a minimum spanning tree (MST) or an odometric backbone (ODOM), then selects additional edges under the same budget.

The pose graph used in this analysis
Actual dataset: synthetic_loop.g2o, 60 poses and 85 edges, plotted directly from the file.

This is the actual graph MAC operates on in these experiments. An ODOM backbone keeps all 59 odometry edges and lets MAC choose from the 26 loop closures under budget. An MST backbone instead starts from a minimum spanning tree over the same candidate edges, so it can occasionally substitute a loop closure for a less useful odometry edge.

What MAC actually selects on this graph
Real output at a 10% edge budget, not a schematic.

These came out of the same MAC implementation used throughout this page, run on a larger real pose graph than the 60-node synthetic_loop.g2o example above (785 candidate loop closures here, versus 26 there). NaiveGreedy and MAC happen to retain the same 78 edges in these particular runs; where they disagree, and by how much, is what the benchmark sweep and the hypotheses below are trying to explain.

Why can the choice of backbone change the outcome of MAC, and can graph structure predict which one will perform better?
02 / The method

Algebraic connectivity, MAC & Frank–Wolfe

Algebraic connectivity (AC) is the second-smallest eigenvalue of the weighted graph Laplacian. A higher value indicates stronger spectral connectivity.

AC(G) = λ2(L)    |    maxx∈𝒳 λ2(L0 + ∑ xiLi)

L₀: backbone Laplacian · Lᵢ: candidate-edge contribution · xᵢ: continuous edge-selection weight · 𝒳: budget-constrained feasible set

Iterative MAC · Frank–Wolfe pseudocodeCONCEPTUAL
INPUT backbone L₀, candidate Laplacians {Lᵢ}, budget K OUTPUT continuous weights x*, then discrete edge set x ← feasible initial weights repeat L(x) ← L₀ + Σᵢ xᵢ Lᵢ (λ₂, v₂) ← second eigenpair of L(x) # Marginal connectivity gain of each candidate gᵢ ← v₂ᵀ Lᵢ v₂ # Frank–Wolfe linear maximization oracle s ← argmax {gᵀs : s ∈ 𝒳} # Update fractional edge weights x ← (1 − γ)x + γs until convergence / iteration limit # Discretization happens after optimization S ← Round(x, K) return backbone ∪ S
Schematic pseudocode, not a verbatim reproduction of the implementation. Gradient expression assumes a simple second eigenvalue; near eigenvalue multiplicity, a subgradient treatment is required.

The optimization landscape

The backbone determines the starting Laplacian and which connectivity weaknesses remain. Frank–Wolfe repeatedly evaluates the Fiedler direction, scores candidate edges, and updates fractional weights. Near-coincident λ₂ and λ₃ values can make the chosen spectral direction sensitive to perturbations. This is an investigated explanation for difficult iterations, not a universally verified failure mechanism.

Why rounding can lose connectivity
Actual convergence behavior of the Frank–Wolfe solver used for this project, including a real bug and its fix.

The early implementation used a fixed diminishing step size and briefly collapsed connectivity at iteration 2 before recovering. Switching to an exact line search (golden-section search over the step size each iteration) removed that dip and converged in about 10 iterations instead of 25–30. Rounding loss, the gap between the relaxed solution MAC converges to here and the discrete graph after rounding, is a separate effect from this convergence behavior; this plot shows the optimizer finding the relaxed optimum, not the rounding step itself.

FAILURE MODE 01

Optimization loss

My continuous solution usually converges below the reference connectivity bound rather than matching it exactly. Part of this traces back to backbone topology, and part to spectral sensitivity: near-coincident λ₂ and λ₃ values can make the climb harder, which is what I ran into with the step-size bug shown in the convergence plot above before I switched to exact line search.

FAILURE MODE 02

Rounding loss

My fractional solution often spreads connectivity benefit thinly across several candidate edges at once. Once I round down to a fixed discrete budget, I can only keep whole edges, so I sometimes lose part of that benefit even when the relaxed solution looked strong. In my benchmark sweep this showed up as MAC matching, not beating, NaiveGreedy at a few budgets (10%, 20%, 100%) even though it won or tied at all ten tested budgets overall.

03 / Observations

What the experiments revealed

Across 14 synthetic and real-world 2D/3D datasets, both backbones were compared over edge budgets and original versus uniform rotational precision (κ).

01

No universal winner

MST leads on some graphs, ODOM on others, and several approach a near tie.

02

Precision can flip the result

Replacing real κ with uniform κ reverses the winner in some datasets, but not all.

03

Two distinct losses

Optimization and rounding errors respond differently to backbone choice and budget.

I ran my fixed MAC solver against NaiveGreedy and a random baseline on a 30-node ring graph with 150 candidate edges, sweeping the edge budget from 10% to 100%. MAC matched or beat NaiveGreedy at all ten budgets I tested, with a +4.4% average improvement in algebraic connectivity. The biggest gain (+23.0%) showed up at a 40% budget; at a few budgets (10%, 20%, 100%) it only matched NaiveGreedy rather than beating it, which is the rounding loss described above in practice. This is a smaller, separate test graph from the one shown earlier, built specifically to validate the solver after the step-size fix, not the datasets from the original research document below.

04 / Hypotheses

What explained the differences, and what didn't

HypothesisResearch finding
Lattice structureNot sufficient on its own. Loop-closure span helps explain why some lattice graphs strongly favor MST while others converge with ODOM.
Precision variation (κ)Can alter MST construction and change the winner, but κ variance alone cannot predict performance.
Effective resistanceUseful for studying which edges enter the backbone and which gaps remain, but not a complete post-MAC explanation.
Graph diameterFails as a reliable predictor: a smaller post-MAC diameter can coexist with lower algebraic connectivity.
Topology & repair capacityTargeted candidate-edge ablations show that a small set of multi-gap repair edges can change the winner. Experimentally supported in the tested case
Spectral sensitivitySmall λ₂–λ₃ gaps and shifting Fiedler directions may affect iterative MAC behavior. Mechanistic hypothesis; further iteration-level validation needed
The research shifted from “Which backbone wins?” to “Where is connectivity lost, and why?”
The outcome reflects an interaction between backbone topology, measurement precision, continuous optimization, candidate repair capacity, and rounding.
